I feel like my firm and the clients are secretly monitoring my every move, just waiting for the right moment to expose me.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever heard voices or seen things that others cannot, which seem to confirm your beliefs about being watched or making a mistake?\n\nPatient: Yes, when I'm alone at my desk or trying to fall asleep, I keep hearing this low, critical voice muttering that I've \"cooked the books\" and \"ruined people's lives.\" It sounds like someone is standing right behind me whispering these things, even though I know the room is completely empty.\n\nDoctor: Do you believe the voice you hear is a part of your own mind or do you think it's an external voice coming from someone or something else?\n\nPatient: It feels completely external, like someone is physically standing right behind me muttering those things. Even though I know the room is empty and quiet, it doesn't sound like my own thoughts at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe any instances where the voice you hear tells you to do something specific, or is it primarily critical comments about your work and perceived mistakes?\n\nPatient: No, it never tells me to do anything. It's just a low, critical voice that mutters accusations about my work, saying things like I've \"cooked the books\" and \"ruined people's lives.\" It usually happens when I'm sitting alone at my desk or trying to fall asleep.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your behavior or daily functioning as a result of these voices and beliefs, such as avoiding certain tasks or social situations?\n\nPatient: Yes, my daily life has completely fallen apart; I've gone from being a reliable accountant to missing deadlines and needing my coworkers to redo my work. I'm also avoiding my friends and have stopped going on hikes, leaving my husband to handle almost all the cooking, bills, and chores because I feel too overwhelmed to do anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the critical voice you hear and your beliefs about being watched and making a mistake could be part of your own mind's worries and fears, or do you firmly believe they are real and coming from outside yourself?\n\nPatient: I am completely convinced that they are real and not just in my head. Despite everyone telling me otherwise, I know there is a real mistake in those books and that I am actually being monitored. That voice whispering behind me is real, and it's not just my imagination or anxiety.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation or evidence that could possibly prove to you that the voice and the feeling of being watched are not real, or are you absolutely certain that they are real no matter what anyone else says or any evidence that might be presented?\n\nPatient: No, there is nothing that could convince me otherwise. Even when I re-check the audit files myself and everything looks fine, I am still absolutely certain the mistake is there and that they are monitoring me. The voice and the feeling of being watched are completely real.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and the voice you hear, could be a product of your own mind, even if it feels completely real to you?\n\nPatient: My husband and manager keep telling me it's not real, and I'm so exhausted that I've had moments of doubting my own judgment. But when I hear that voice whispering right behind me, it feels so terrifyingly real that I just can't believe it's only in my head. In those moments, I am absolutely certain there is a mistake and that they are watching me.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where you had to make a decision based on your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and how did that turn out for you?\n\nPatient: Recently, I was trying to finalize a basic report but was too terrified to submit it because I was certain there was a hidden mistake and that the clients were watching me. I ended up breaking down in a meeting and admitting I couldn't trust my own judgment anymore, which is why my manager and husband convinced me to seek help.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when the voice you hear or the feelings of being watched have been proven wrong, or do they always seem to be correct in your mind?\n\nPatient: No, they always seem completely correct to me. Even when my manager reassures me and I re-check the files myself, I remain absolutely certain that the mistake is real and that I'm being monitored. The voice and the feeling of being watched just feel too real for me to believe any reassurance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a moment, no matter how brief, where you questioned the reality of the voice or the belief that you're being watched, or has your conviction in their reality been constant?\n\nPatient: My conviction has felt constant and absolute, and whenever they are active, I don't doubt that the voice and the monitoring are entirely real. However, on a couple of rare days when my heavy mood lifted slightly, those paranoid thoughts and the voice actually faded into the background and disappeared. But as soon as the darkness returns, I am completely certain of them again.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel completely normal and free from these thoughts and voices, or are they always present to some degree?\n\nPatient: I never experienced these voices or paranoid thoughts before this deep depression and dread started seven months ago. Now, they are almost always with me, though on the rare, brief days when my mood lifts even a little bit, the voice and the feeling of being watched actually fade into the background and disappear.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned having moments where your mood lifts and the voice and feelings of being watched fade away. During those moments, do you ever wonder if your beliefs about the mistake and being monitored might not be entirely true, or is your conviction in their reality unwavering even then?\n\nPatient: Yes, during those brief moments when the heavy cloud lifts, I get a little distance from the panic and start to think that maybe it isn't actually real. But as soon as that dark mood returns, the absolute conviction that I've ruined everything comes right back with full force.\n\nDoctor: When you're experiencing those rare moments of slightly improved mood and the voices and paranoid thoughts fade, do you still believe in the reality of the mistake and being watched, or do you start to question those beliefs during those times?\n\nPatient: Yes, during those brief times when my mood lifts, I actually start to question those beliefs and think they might not be real at all. It's like I can finally step back and realize that maybe I didn't actually ruin everything. But as soon as the heavy depression returns, that clarity completely vanishes and they feel 100% real again.\n\nDoctor: Can you explain what you think would happen if you were to discover conclusive evidence that there was no mistake in the books and no one was monitoring you, would that change your beliefs about the voice and the feeling of being watched?\n\nPatient: I don't think any evidence would actually change my mind, because the voice and the monitoring just feel too real to be dismissed by logic. Even if I were shown absolute proof, I would still be convinced that the mistake exists and that they are watching me. The only time that certainty ever wavers is on those rare days when my heavy mood briefly lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any difference between the times when you're certain of the mistake and being watched, and those brief moments when your mood improves and you question those beliefs?\n\nPatient: The main difference is just the weight of my depression. Before this deep dread started seven months ago, I never had these thoughts or heard the voices at all. Now, on the rare days when my heavy mood lifts slightly, the voices and the feeling of being watched fade into the background and disappear entirely.\n\nDoctor: During those moments when your mood improves and you start to question the reality of the voice and the feeling of being watched, do you think your improved mood is what allows you to see things more clearly, or is it the other way around - that questioning those beliefs is what helps improve your mood?\n\nPatient: It definitely feels like the improvement in my mood is what drives the change. On those rare days when the heavy dread lifts slightly, the paranoid thoughts and the voice just seem to naturally fade into the background on their own. I'm not actively trying to question or dispute them to make myself feel better; they just disappear when the weight lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your perception of the voice and the feeling of being watched changes when your mood improves, and do you think this change is due to the improvement in your mood or something else?"

It's just a low, critical voice that mutters accusations about my work, saying things like I've \"cooked the books\" and \"ruined people's lives.\" It usually happens when I'm sitting alone at my desk or trying to fall asleep.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your behavior or daily functioning as a result of these voices and beliefs, such as avoiding certain tasks or social situations?\n\nPatient: Yes, my daily life has completely fallen apart; I've gone from being a reliable accountant to missing deadlines and needing my coworkers to redo my work. I'm also avoiding my friends and have stopped going on hikes, leaving my husband to handle almost all the cooking, bills, and chores because I feel too overwhelmed to do anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the critical voice you hear and your beliefs about being watched and making a mistake could be part of your own mind's worries and fears, or do you firmly believe they are real and coming from outside yourself?\n\nPatient: I am completely convinced that they are real and not just in my head. Despite everyone telling me otherwise, I know there is a real mistake in those books and that I am actually being monitored. That voice whispering behind me is real, and it's not just my imagination or anxiety.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation or evidence that could possibly prove to you that the voice and the feeling of being watched are not real, or are you absolutely certain that they are real no matter what anyone else says or any evidence that might be presented?\n\nPatient: No, there is nothing that could convince me otherwise. Even when I re-check the audit files myself and everything looks fine, I am still absolutely certain the mistake is there and that they are monitoring me. The voice and the feeling of being watched are completely real.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and the voice you hear, could be a product of your own mind, even if it feels completely real to you?\n\nPatient: My husband and manager keep telling me it's not real, and I'm so exhausted that I've had moments of doubting my own judgment. But when I hear that voice whispering right behind me, it feels so terrifyingly real that I just can't believe it's only in my head. In those moments, I am absolutely certain there is a mistake and that they are watching me.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where you had to make a decision based on your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and how did that turn out for you?\n\nPatient: Recently, I was trying to finalize a basic report but was too terrified to submit it because I was certain there was a hidden mistake and that the clients were watching me. I ended up breaking down in a meeting and admitting I couldn't trust my own judgment anymore, which is why my manager and husband convinced me to seek help.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when the voice you hear or the feelings of being watched have been proven wrong, or do they always seem to be correct in your mind?\n\nPatient: No, they always seem completely correct to me. Even when my manager reassures me and I re-check the files myself, I remain absolutely certain that the mistake is real and that I'm being monitored. The voice and the feeling of being watched just feel too real for me to believe any reassurance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a moment, no matter how brief, where you questioned the reality of the voice or the belief that you're being watched, or has your conviction in their reality been constant?\n\nPatient: My conviction has felt constant and absolute, and whenever they are active, I don't doubt that the voice and the monitoring are entirely real. But as soon as the heavy depression returns, that clarity completely vanishes and they feel 100% real again.\n\nDoctor: Can you explain what you think would happen if you were to discover conclusive evidence that there was no mistake in the books and no one was monitoring you, would that change your beliefs about the voice and the feeling of being watched?\n\nPatient: I don't think any evidence would actually change my mind, because the voice and the monitoring just feel too real to be dismissed by logic. On those rare days when the heavy dread lifts slightly, the paranoid thoughts and the voice just seem to naturally fade into the background on their own. I'm not actively trying to question or dispute them to make myself feel better; they just disappear when the weight lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your perception of the voice and the feeling of being watched changes when your mood improves, and do you think this change is due to the improvement in your mood or something else?\n\nPatient: When my mood lifts even a little bit, the critical voice and the feeling of being watched fade into the background or disappear entirely. I definitely think it is directly tied to how low my mood is, because before this heavy depression and dread started seven months ago, I never heard those voices or felt monitored at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you could imagine the voice and the feeling of being watched being a product of your own mind, perhaps as a manifestation of your anxiety or depression, rather than an external reality?\n\nPatient: When I'm in the middle of it, the voice and the feeling of being watched feel so terrifyingly real that it's almost impossible to doubt them. It's just incredibly hard to hold onto that logic when the darkness returns and they feel so real again.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your depression is contributing to your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and that the voice you hear might be a symptom of your mental state rather than an external reality?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've actually started to notice that connection myself. I don't think it's a way of coping, though, because it feels more like my mind is punishing me when I'm down. When the heavy dread returns, that understanding slips away and they feel completely real and terrifying again."

But as soon as the heavy depression returns, that clarity completely vanishes and they feel 100% real again.\n\nDoctor: Can you explain what you think would happen if you were to discover conclusive evidence that there was no mistake in the books and no one was monitoring you, would that change your beliefs about the voice and the feeling of being watched?\n\nPatient: I don't think any evidence would actually change my mind, because the voice and the monitoring just feel too real to be dismissed by logic. Even if I were shown absolute proof, I would still be convinced that the mistake exists and that they are watching me. The only time that certainty ever wavers is on those rare days when my heavy mood briefly lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any difference between the times when you're certain of the mistake and being watched, and those brief moments when your mood improves and you question those beliefs?\n\nPatient: The main difference is just the weight of my depression. Before this deep dread started seven months ago, I never had these thoughts or heard the voices at all. Now, on the rare days when my heavy mood lifts slightly, the voices and the feeling of being watched fade into the background and disappear entirely.\n\nDoctor: During those moments when your mood improves and you start to question the reality of the voice and the feeling of being watched, do you think your improved mood is what allows you to see things more clearly, or is it the other way around - that questioning those beliefs is what helps improve your mood?\n\nPatient: It definitely feels like the improvement in my mood is what drives the change. On those rare days when the heavy dread lifts slightly, the paranoid thoughts and the voice just seem to naturally fade into the background on their own. I'm not actively trying to question or dispute them to make myself feel better; they just disappear when the weight lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your perception of the voice and the feeling of being watched changes when your mood improves, and do you think this change is due to the improvement in your mood or something else?\n\nPatient: When my mood lifts even a little bit, the critical voice and the feeling of being watched fade into the background or disappear entirely. I definitely think it is directly tied to how low my mood is, because before this heavy depression and dread started seven months ago, I never heard those voices or felt monitored at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you could imagine the voice and the feeling of being watched being a product of your own mind, perhaps as a manifestation of your anxiety or depression, rather than an external reality?\n\nPatient: When I'm in the middle of it, the voice and the feeling of being watched feel so terrifyingly real that it's almost impossible to doubt them. It's just a low, critical voice that mutters accusations about my work, saying things like I've \"cooked the books\" and \"ruined people's lives.\" It usually happens when I'm sitting alone at my desk or trying to fall asleep.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any significant changes in your behavior or daily functioning as a result of these voices and beliefs, such as avoiding certain tasks or social situations?\n\nPatient: Yes, my daily life has completely fallen apart; I've gone from being a reliable accountant to missing deadlines and needing my coworkers to redo my work. I'm also avoiding my friends and have stopped going on hikes, leaving my husband to handle almost all the cooking, bills, and chores because I feel too overwhelmed to do anything.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the critical voice you hear and your beliefs about being watched and making a mistake could be part of your own mind's worries and fears, or do you firmly believe they are real and coming from outside yourself?\n\nPatient: I am completely convinced that they are real and not just in my head. Despite everyone telling me otherwise, I know there is a real mistake in those books and that I am actually being monitored. That voice whispering behind me is real, and it's not just my imagination or anxiety.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation or evidence that could possibly prove to you that the voice and the feeling of being watched are not real, or are you absolutely certain that they are real no matter what anyone else says or any evidence that might be presented?\n\nPatient: No, there is nothing that could convince me otherwise. Even when I re-check the audit files myself and everything looks fine, I am still absolutely certain the mistake is there and that they are monitoring me. The voice and the feeling of being watched are completely real.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and the voice you hear, could be a product of your own mind, even if it feels completely real to you?\n\nPatient: My husband and manager keep telling me it's not real, and I'm so exhausted that I've had moments of doubting my own judgment. But when I hear that voice whispering right behind me, it feels so terrifyingly real that I just can't believe it's only in my head. In those moments, I am absolutely certain there is a mistake and that they are watching me.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe a recent situation where you had to make a decision based on your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and how did that turn out for you?\n\nPatient: Recently, I was trying to finalize a basic report but was too terrified to submit it because I was certain there was a hidden mistake and that the clients were watching me. I ended up breaking down in a meeting and admitting I couldn't trust my own judgment anymore, which is why my manager and husband convinced me to seek help.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any times when the voice you hear or the feelings of being watched have been proven wrong, or do they always seem to be correct in your mind?\n\nPatient: No, they always seem completely correct to me. Even when my manager reassures me and I re-check the files myself, I remain absolutely certain that the mistake is real and that I'm being monitored. The voice and the feeling of being watched just feel too real for me to believe any reassurance.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a moment, no matter how brief, where you questioned the reality of the voice or the belief that you're being watched, or has your conviction in their reality been constant?\n\nPatient: My conviction has felt constant and absolute, and whenever they are active, I don't doubt that the voice and the monitoring are entirely real. However, on a couple of rare days when my heavy mood lifted slightly, those paranoid thoughts and the voice actually faded into the background and disappeared. But as soon as the darkness returns, I am completely certain of them again.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me if there are any times when you feel completely normal and free from these thoughts and voices, or are they always present to some degree?\n\nPatient: I never experienced these voices or paranoid thoughts before this deep depression and dread started seven months ago. Now, they are almost always with me, though on the rare, brief days when my mood lifts even a little bit, the voice and the feeling of being watched actually fade into the background and disappear.\n\nDoctor: You've mentioned having moments where your mood lifts and the voice and feelings of being watched fade away. During those moments, do you ever wonder if your beliefs about the mistake and being monitored might not be entirely true, or is your conviction in their reality unwavering even then?\n\nPatient: Yes, during those brief moments when the heavy cloud lifts, I get a little distance from the panic and start to think that maybe it isn't actually real. But as soon as that dark mood returns, the absolute conviction that I've ruined everything comes right back with full force.\n\nDoctor: When you're experiencing those rare moments of slightly improved mood and the voices and paranoid thoughts fade, do you still believe in the reality of the mistake and being watched, or do you start to question those beliefs during those times?\n\nPatient: Yes, during those brief times when my mood lifts, I actually start to question those beliefs and think they might not be real at all. It's like I can finally step back and realize that maybe I didn't actually ruin everything. But as soon as the heavy depression returns, that clarity completely vanishes and they feel 100% real again.\n\nDoctor: Can you explain what you think would happen if you were to discover conclusive evidence that there was no mistake in the books and no one was monitoring you, would that change your beliefs about the voice and the feeling of being watched?\n\nPatient: I don't think any evidence would actually change my mind, because the voice and the monitoring just feel too real to be dismissed by logic. Even if I were shown absolute proof, I would still be convinced that the mistake exists and that they are watching me. The only time that certainty ever wavers is on those rare days when my heavy mood briefly lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any difference between the times when you're certain of the mistake and being watched, and those brief moments when your mood improves and you question those beliefs?\n\nPatient: The main difference is just the weight of my depression. Before this deep dread started seven months ago, I never had these thoughts or heard the voices at all. Now, on the rare days when my heavy mood lifts slightly, the voices and the feeling of being watched fade into the background and disappear entirely.\n\nDoctor: During those moments when your mood improves and you start to question the reality of the voice and the feeling of being watched, do you think your improved mood is what allows you to see things more clearly, or is it the other way around - that questioning those beliefs is what helps improve your mood?\n\nPatient: It definitely feels like the improvement in my mood is what drives the change. On those rare days when the heavy dread lifts slightly, the paranoid thoughts and the voice just seem to naturally fade into the background on their own. I'm not actively trying to question or dispute them to make myself feel better; they just disappear when the weight lifts.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe how your perception of the voice and the feeling of being watched changes when your mood improves, and do you think this change is due to the improvement in your mood or something else?\n\nPatient: When my mood lifts even a little bit, the critical voice and the feeling of being watched fade into the background or disappear entirely. I definitely think it is directly tied to how low my mood is, because before this heavy depression and dread started seven months ago, I never heard those voices or felt monitored at all.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any situation where you could imagine the voice and the feeling of being watched being a product of your own mind, perhaps as a manifestation of your anxiety or depression, rather than an external reality?\n\nPatient: When I'm in the middle of it, the voice and the feeling of being watched feel so terrifyingly real that it's almost impossible to doubt them. But because they only started when this heavy depression set in, and they completely vanish on the rare days my mood lifts, I do wonder if they are somehow connected to my mental state. It's just incredibly hard to hold onto that logic when the darkness returns and they feel so real again.\n\nDoctor: Do you think it's possible that your depression is contributing to your beliefs about the mistake and being watched, and that the voice you hear might be a symptom of your mental state rather than an external reality?\n\nPatient: Yes, I've actually started to notice that connection myself. Before this heavy depression and dread started, I never heard the voice or felt like I was being watched. Since they both fade away on the rare days my mood lifts even slightly, it really makes me think they might indeed be tied to my depression.\n\nDoctor: When you are not experiencing the voice or feeling of being watched, do you think it's possible that your mind is playing a role in creating those experiences, perhaps as a way of coping with your depression or anxiety?\n\nPatient: During those brief moments of relief when my mood lifts, I can start to see how closely tied those experiences are to my depression. I don't think it's a way of coping, though, because it feels more like my mind is punishing me when I'm down. When the heavy dread returns, that understanding slips away and they feel completely real and terrifying again.\n\nDoctor: Can you describe if the voice you hear and the feelings of being watched seem to be directly related to your mood, meaning they are worse when you're more depressed and better when your mood improves?\n\nPatient: Yes, they are directly tied to how depressed I feel. I never experienced these voices or the feeling of being watched before this heavy depression started, and on the rare days when my mood lifts even slightly, they disappear completely.\n\nDoctor: When you're in a period where your mood has improved and the voices and feelings of being watched have faded, do you think you could be persuaded that your beliefs about the mistake and being monitored might not be entirely true, or would you still hold onto them even then?\n\nPatient: On those brief days when my mood lifts slightly, the paranoid thoughts and the voice disappear entirely, so I don't really hold onto those beliefs because the feelings themselves go away. But as soon as the heavy depression returns, the absolute certainty about the mistakes and being monitored comes right back.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any ways to test the reality of the voice and the feeling of being watched when you're in a better mood, to see if they might be connected to your depression rather than an external reality?\n\nPatient: I'm not really sure how I would set up a test, but I have noticed a clear pattern where the voice and the feelings of being watched completely disappear on the rare days my mood lifts slightly. Even though they feel terrifyingly real and convincing when I'm depressed, seeing them fade away like that makes me realize they might indeed be tied to my mental state.\n\nDoctor: Do you think that if you were able to manage your depression effectively, the voice and the feeling of being watched might also decrease or disappear, indicating they are more closely tied to your mental state than to an external reality?\n\nPatient: Yes, I really believe managing the depression would make them go away, because I've noticed myself how closely tied they are to my mood. Before this heavy depression and dread started, I never heard those accusing voices or felt monitored at all. On the rare, brief days when my mood lifts even slightly, those paranoid thoughts and the voice fade into the background or disappear entirely.\n\nDoctor: Can you think of any ways that your current treatment for depression, if started, might affect the voice you hear and the feelings of being watched, considering how they seem to be connected to your mood?\n\nPatient: I really hope that treating the depression will help make them go away, as they seem so closely tied to how low I feel.
